route: iOS Contacts framework (CNContactStore) read, with full or user-limited authorization
required_permission: Contacts authorization via CNContactStore requestAccess(for:). On iOS 18+ the person chooses full access or a chosen subset (CNAuthorizationStatus.limited) and can change it later in Settings.
data_scope: Address-book records the app is allowed to see: names, phone numbers, emails, dates such as birthdays, and so on (exact field list not re-verified this session). With limited access, only the contacts the person picked.
historical_coverage: The address book's current state only. There is no interaction or communication history.
refresh_cadence: On demand while the app runs. Change-tracking APIs were not verified this session.
restrictions: App Review 5.1.1(iii): use the out-of-process picker where possible instead of full access. 5.1.2(iv): Contacts data must not be used to build a contact database for the app's own use or for sale. 5.1.2(v): the app may contact people only at the user's explicit, individual initiative.
next_experiment: Spike: call requestAccess, handle .limited by showing ContactAccessButton, and read the selected contacts' birthdays and anniversaries into the on-device store. Confirm what the app sees after the person adds more contacts in Settings.
evidence_notes: The ContactAccessButton docs say people 'can choose to give the app full access to their contacts or to a subset of contacts' on the first requestAccess and can update that in Settings. App Review 5.1.1(iii) recommends the out-of-process picker over full access to Contacts.

route: EventKit EKEventStore with requestFullAccessToEvents (iOS 17+)
required_permission: Full calendar access, with the NSCalendarsFullAccessUsageDescription key in Info.plist. On iOS 17+, a missing key, or only the legacy NSCalendarsUsageDescription, makes iOS deny the request automatically.
data_scope: Create, view, edit and delete events across the device's calendars. Attendee fields are expected but were not re-verified this session.
historical_coverage: Whatever the calendars synced to the device contain. Limits on query ranges were not verified.
refresh_cadence: On demand while the app runs, plus best-effort background refresh. Store-change notifications were not verified this session.
restrictions: There is no read-only option: 'To read events or reminders from the event store, your app needs full access.' Sandboxed macOS apps need the com.apple.security.personal-information.calendars entitlement.
next_experiment: Spike: request full access, query the last 12 months of events, match attendees to contacts by email or phone, and compute each person's meeting cadence on-device. Time the query on a calendar with about 5k events.
evidence_notes: Apple says full access 'lets your app create, view, edit, and delete data', and that reading events needs full access. iOS 17+ needs the new usage-description keys or 'iOS automatically denies any access request'.

route: EventKit write-only access (requestWriteOnlyAccessToEvents), or the EventKitUI editor with no permission at all
required_permission: NSCalendarsWriteOnlyAccessUsageDescription for write-only access. EventKitUI (EKEventEditViewController) needs no calendar permission on iOS 17+.
data_scope: Create events only. Write-only access 'doesn't let it read any events or other calendar information, including events your app created'. A calendar listing returns one virtual calendar.
restrictions: None found. Apple advises requesting only the access a feature needs.
next_experiment: Use EKEventEditViewController for flows like 'add birthday reminder' or 'schedule coffee', and confirm on iOS 26 that no permission prompt appears.
evidence_notes: EventKitUI 'presents chooser and editor UI outside of your app's process on iOS 17 and later', and an app 'can use EventKitUI without requesting write-only or full calendar access.'

route: LinkedIn self-serve OAuth permissions: Sign In with LinkedIn using OpenID Connect (profile, email) and Share on LinkedIn (w_member_social)
required_permission: profile, email and w_member_social, added self-serve on the Developer Portal Products tab.
data_scope: The signed-in member's own name, headline, photo and primary email, plus posting, commenting and liking as that member. No connections, feed or messages.
restrictions: These are the only permissions open to every developer; 'Most permissions and partner programs require explicit approval'. In the documented 3-legged flow the token exchange needs client_secret, and LinkedIn says to keep it secure. PKCE for native apps is not documented on the pages fetched.
next_experiment: None for capture. Only if a 'share to LinkedIn' feature is wanted: ask LinkedIn developer support whether a public client (PKCE, no client_secret) is allowed.
evidence_notes: Getting Access lists the open consumer permissions as profile and email (OIDC) plus w_member_social, and says other programs are gated. The Authorization Code Flow page lists client_secret as Required in the access-token request.

route: LinkedIn Connections API (r_1st_connections) or Compliance APIs (r_compliance)
required_permission: r_1st_connections (not among the open permissions) or r_compliance (the Compliance program is 'closed and may not be requested').
data_scope: List of 1st-degree connections (from a search-result snippet of the Connections API doc; the page itself was not opened).
restrictions: Needs partner approval. Compliance is closed. The snippet notes connection data is subject to members' privacy settings.
next_experiment: None. Do not pursue unless a LinkedIn partnership becomes a business goal.
evidence_notes: Getting Access shows that Compliance permissions (r_compliance) are 'closed and may not be requested', and that r_1st_connections is not an open permission. The Connections API snippet says it needs r_1st_connections or r_compliance.

route: LinkedIn Member Data Portability (3rd Party) API under the EU DMA: Member Snapshot API and Member Changelog API
required_permission: r_dma_portability_3rd_party through 3-legged OAuth. The developer app needs a LinkedIn Company Page with a verified association, business verification (business email, legal name, registered address, website, privacy policy) and LinkedIn review of the access request.
data_scope: Snapshot domains include CONNECTIONS ('Name, position, company, and connection date of 1st degree connections'), INBOX ('Messages sent and received in the member's inbox'), PROFILE, POSITIONS, INVITATIONS, MEMBER_SHARE_INFO, PREMIUM_NOTES and more. The Changelog covers the member's own interactions (posts, comments, reactions).
historical_coverage: Snapshot: historical data processed after consent; 'Data for certain domains will be available sooner than others'. Changelog: only events after consent, and only the past 28 days can be queried.
refresh_cadence: Snapshot on demand. The Changelog must be polled at least every 28 days to avoid gaps.
restrictions: Only LinkedIn members in the EEA can consent (3rd-party doc). The help center says EU/EEA or Switzerland, based on profile location. Personal email addresses fail business verification. The token exchange needs client_secret. The API needs the header Linkedin-Version: 202312.
next_experiment: Product decision: an EEA-only feature would need (a) LinkedIn business verification and (b) a token-exchange service holding client_secret, which is a backend and conflicts with current constraints. Meanwhile, ask LinkedIn whether a public client (PKCE) is allowed for r_dma_portability_3rd_party.
evidence_notes: The only DMA route found that exposes connections and inbox messages. LinkedIn says 'Only LinkedIn users from the European Economic Area are allowed to consent', and access requires a verified Company Page plus business verification. Because CONNECTIONS includes each connection's current position and company, comparing snapshots would surface job changes.

route: User-requested LinkedIn data archive ('Get a copy of your data'), imported through Files or the share sheet
required_permission: None from LinkedIn's API. The member requests the archive at Settings & Privacy > Data privacy > Get a copy of your data. The app needs a file importer (document picker or share extension).
data_scope: Connections in CSV or vCard. Expected fields are name, company, position and connection date, inferred from the DMA CONNECTIONS domain; the exact columns of Connections.csv are not verified. An email address appears only if that connection allows it. The larger archive includes 'connections, verifications, contacts, account history'; whether it includes messages is not verified.
historical_coverage: Point-in-time snapshot at export. The connection date gives when each relationship started.
refresh_cadence: Manual: only when the user exports again. Must be labelled a manual import, never automatic monitoring.
restrictions: 'The CSV and vCard formats don't support all characters' (Chinese, Japanese and Hebrew are listed as unsupported). Only 1st-degree connections.
next_experiment: Request a real archive from a test account and record the exact file names and columns. Write an on-device parser, then compare two exports taken about a month apart to detect job or company changes.
evidence_notes: The help center gives the steps; the download link arrives by email to the primary address. It warns that emails show only for connections who allow it and that CSV/vCard don't support every character set.

route: Facebook Login with the Graph API user_friends permission
required_permission: user_friends. Whether App Review applies was not shown in the fetched excerpt.
data_scope: 'a list of a person's friends using that app', meaning only friends who also use LittleThings. No permission in the reference grants friends' posts (user_posts covers only the user's own timeline).
restrictions: Allowed usage: 'Provide Facebook-related content to personalize a person's experience.'
next_experiment: None. It cannot return the user's social graph or friends' life updates.
evidence_notes: The Permissions Reference says user_friends 'allows your app to get a list of a person's friends using that app.' The claim that friends' posts can't be read is an inference: no permission listed grants them.

route: Graph API user_posts (the user's own timeline posts)
required_permission: user_posts
data_scope: 'the posts that a user has made on their timeline'.
restrictions: Allowed usage is limited to making physical or digital books or albums of timelines, and parental monitoring of under-18 dependents. A relationship-assistant use case is not listed.
next_experiment: None. The use case does not match the allowed usage.
evidence_notes: The Permissions Reference lists allowed usage for user_posts as timeline books or albums and parental monitoring only.

route: Meta Accounts Center 'Export your information' (Download Your Information) to the device in JSON, then imported into the app
required_permission: None from an API. The user creates a password-protected export and shares the ZIP into LittleThings.
data_scope: 'content and info you've shared, your activity and info we collect'. Category names (Messages, Friends and so on) and the message JSON schema were not verified this session.
historical_coverage: The user picks a date range, so the full history is possible.
refresh_cadence: Manual. A finished export can be downloaded for 4 days.
restrictions: None found in the fetched pages. HTML or JSON format; media quality affects file size.
next_experiment: Export JSON from a test account with Messages and Friends selected. Document the folder layout and the message JSON fields (sender, timestamp, content, text encoding are all not verified), then build an on-device parser.
evidence_notes: The Facebook Help Center describes the flow: Accounts Center > Your information and permissions > Export your information > Export to device, choosing info, date range, format and media quality. JSON is 'A machine readable format', and the export stays available for 4 days.

route: Meta Data Portability (DMA): become a destination in Export Your Information using the Data Transfer Project
required_permission: A Level 1 or Level 2 entry in the DTI Trust Registry, a verified Meta Business Manager account, a public privacy policy, an OAuth 2.0 authorization server, and Meta's onboarding review.
data_scope: DTP data types are not listed on the fetched pages; photos are the example. Posts and messages are not mentioned.
restrictions: Meta pushes data to the destination: 'Meta's portability infrastructure needs to call your APIs on behalf of the user'. The destination must host write APIs (for example POST /V1/photo) and OAuth. Eligible regions not stated.
next_experiment: None under current constraints. Record it as a hard backend dependency, and check again if Meta publishes a pull-style DMA API.
evidence_notes: The EU DMA portal lists Meta's resources as the end-user DYI tool and the 'Data Portability Developer Guide'. That guide describes Meta's DTP worker calling the destination's hosted APIs, which needs a server.

route: Instagram API (Instagram Login, Facebook Login or Unified Login), including messaging and webhooks
required_permission: An Instagram professional (Business or Creator) account. The Facebook Login route also needs a linked Facebook Page. App Review details were not verified.
data_scope: For professional accounts: publishing, comments, mentions, insights, messaging, and webhooks for real-time notifications. Nothing is documented for personal accounts or for reading other users' feeds.
refresh_cadence: Webhooks deliver to a server (not applicable).
restrictions: The Instagram Basic Display API ended on December 4, 2024: 'there will no longer be a set of Instagram APIs for consumer developer apps.'
next_experiment: None. There is no consumer or personal-account API.
evidence_notes: Meta's blog: 'Starting on December 4th, 2024, Instagram Basic Display API will no longer be available'. The replacements target business and creator accounts only.

route: Instagram 'Export your information' through Meta Accounts Center, imported into the app
required_permission: None from an API. The user creates the export in Accounts Center and shares the file into LittleThings.
data_scope: Expected to match the Meta Accounts Center export (HTML or JSON). Instagram-specific categories (messages, followers/following) are not verified: the Instagram help page could not be fetched.
historical_coverage: The user picks a date range (per the Accounts Center flow; Instagram-specific behavior not verified).
restrictions: Not verified.
next_experiment: Export JSON from a test Instagram account (messages, followers, following), document the schema, and reuse the Meta DYI parser.
evidence_notes: Only the Facebook help article on the shared Accounts Center export was readable. https://help.instagram.com/181231772500920 came back empty, so the Instagram-specific details are unverified.

route: Gmail API called directly from the iOS app, with Google OAuth for installed apps (PKCE, no client secret)
required_permission: gmail.metadata or gmail.readonly; both are classified 'Restricted'. A public launch needs restricted-scope OAuth app verification. A CASA security assessment applies only 'If you store or transmit restricted scope data on servers'.
data_scope: gmail.metadata: headers and labels. gmail.readonly: full messages. (The scope semantics come from the scope names and were not re-read in detail.)
historical_coverage: Expected to cover the whole mailbox through paging (not re-verified).
refresh_cadence: Opportunistic: when the app opens, plus best-effort BGAppRefresh. Gmail server push was not investigated and would likely need cloud infrastructure.
restrictions: Apps in development or testing are exempt from verification but subject to a user cap. The Limited Use policy applies. A security assessment, if required, is renewed at least every 12 months.
next_experiment: Create an iOS OAuth client in a test Google Cloud project (testing mode) and sign in with AppAuth or Google Sign-In using gmail.metadata. Fetch 90 days of headers on-device and compute per-contact cadence. Then file for restricted-scope verification and confirm that no CASA is needed because there is no server.
evidence_notes: The scopes page marks gmail.readonly and gmail.metadata Restricted, and requires a security assessment only when data is stored on or sent through servers. The native-app OAuth page says installed apps 'cannot keep secrets', recommends always using PKCE, and says client_secret 'is not applicable' for iOS clients.

route: Microsoft Graph /me/messages with delegated permissions from a public client (MSAL) on the device
required_permission: Mail.ReadBasic (least privileged), or Mail.Read or Mail.ReadWrite. Delegated permissions work for both work/school and personal Microsoft accounts. Admin-consent requirements for the Mail.* permissions were not verified (the permissions reference was truncated when read).
data_scope: Messages in the signed-in user's mailbox. Bodies come back as HTML by default (a Prefer header can switch to text). Whether Mail.ReadBasic excludes bodies was not verified.
historical_coverage: The whole mailbox through paging ($top from 1 to 1000).
refresh_cadence: Opportunistic or best-effort background. Delta queries were not verified.
restrictions: Work tenants may restrict user consent (not verified).
next_experiment: Register a multi-tenant public-client app that also allows personal accounts. Sign in with MSAL on iOS, list 90 days with $select=from,toRecipients,sentDateTime,subject, and check the consent screens for an outlook.com account and a default Microsoft 365 tenant.
evidence_notes: List messages names Mail.ReadBasic as least privileged for both 'Delegated (work or school account)' and 'Delegated (personal Microsoft account)'. The Exchange OAuth page says MSAL client libraries can 'fetch an access token from your client application.'

route: Generic IMAP with SASL XOAUTH2 (Outlook.com and Microsoft 365; Gmail through the https://mail.google.com/ scope)
required_permission: Microsoft: https://outlook.office.com/IMAP.AccessAsUser.All, plus offline_access for refresh tokens. Google: https://mail.google.com/ (Restricted, same verification as the Gmail API). Other providers were not investigated; avoid app-password flows, which mean handling credentials.
data_scope: The full mailbox over IMAP.
refresh_cadence: Only while the app runs or during best-effort background time. Persistent IMAP IDLE in the iOS background was not verified and is unlikely.
restrictions: Microsoft OAuth2 for IMAP 'is available for both Microsoft 365 ... and Outlook.com users.' The Google restricted-scope rules apply.
next_experiment: Only if the Graph or Gmail REST APIs fall short: test XOAUTH2 against outlook.office365.com and imap.gmail.com with an on-device IMAP library, and compare battery and latency with the REST APIs.
evidence_notes: Microsoft documents the IMAP scope string and the XOAUTH2 SASL format. Google lists https://mail.google.com/ as a Restricted scope.

route: Mac companion Mail extension (MailKit message action handler) observing messages as Apple Mail downloads them
required_permission: The user enables the Mail extension in Mail (the enablement flow was not verified). macOS 12+.
data_scope: MEMessage gives from, to, cc, bcc, subject, dateSent, dateReceived, headers, and rawData ('The raw RFC 2822 header and body content'; rawData is optional and when it is nil is undocumented).
historical_coverage: Unclear. Action handlers run 'when Mail downloads messages' (new mail). No bulk history access is documented.
refresh_cadence: Event-driven while Mail runs on the Mac.
restrictions: macOS only, and only for people who use Apple Mail on a Mac. Getting results to the iPhone without a product backend needs a design decision, for example the user's own iCloud private database (not investigated).
next_experiment: Build a MailKit extension on macOS 26 that logs MEMessage headers for incoming mail. Check whether rawData is populated and whether the handler sees messages from every account.
evidence_notes: MailKit lists macOS 12.0 as its only platform. A message action handler 'performs actions such as flagging, setting colors, or archiving when Mail downloads messages'.

route: Reading Apple Mail on iPhone
required_permission: Not applicable.
data_scope: None.
restrictions: MailKit is macOS-only. No iOS API for reading Mail data was found.
next_experiment: None. Use Gmail, Graph or IMAP OAuth for the underlying account instead.
evidence_notes: MailKit's platform list shows only macOS 12.0.

route: A third-party iOS app reading Messages (iMessage or SMS) history
required_permission: Not applicable.
data_scope: None.
restrictions: No public API. Apple DTS points only to TelephonyMessagingKit, which has its own limits (see imessage-sms-telephonymessagingkit).
next_experiment: File an enhancement request through Feedback Assistant, as DTS suggests, describing a consented, on-device, per-contact metadata read. Nothing to build.
evidence_notes: DTS (thread 804040): 'macOS doesn't have an API for accessing the user's SMS messages' and, for iOS, TelephonyMessagingKit 'comes with its own limitations'. The TelephonyMessagingKit docs describe no access to existing history or to iMessage.

route: TelephonyMessagingKit: LittleThings becomes the user's default carrier messaging app (SMS, MMS, RCS)
required_permission: The com.apple.developer.carrier-messaging-app entitlement, and the user must select the app as default carrier messaging app. Check TelephonyMessagingSession.isConfiguredForCarrierMessaging before use.
data_scope: While the app is the default, 'the system sends all SMS, MMS, and RCS messages received by the device to your app', and the app can send through smsService, mmsService and rcsService. iMessage is not covered.
historical_coverage: Only messages queued while the app wasn't running, plus new ones. Earlier history is not described. Queued messages 'may' be discarded if the app doesn't fetch them in time.
refresh_cadence: Real time: the system launches the app in the background when a message arrives.
restrictions: iOS 26+, iPhone only. 'People using your app must have an account registered in the European Union (EU), and their device must be located within the EU.' LittleThings would have to become a full replacement SMS/RCS client.
next_experiment: Product decision only. An EU-only full SMS client is outside the product's scope; revisit if Apple expands the regions. If it is ever pursued, develop with the Apple-provided provisioning profile, which works in all regions for testing.
evidence_notes: The framework is for the default carrier messaging app and sends and receives 'standards-based messages over cellular networks'. Users must be EU-registered and in the EU. This is the only documented programmatic SMS send route on iOS.

route: Default (internet) messaging app entitlement, com.apple.developer.messaging-app (iOS 18.2+)
required_permission: The com.apple.developer.messaging-app entitlement plus the im: URL scheme.
data_scope: It lets the app open im: links as the default messaging app. Nothing on the page grants access to Messages or iMessage data.
restrictions: The page mentions no regional limits. It is for apps that are themselves messaging services.
next_experiment: None.
evidence_notes: 'In iOS and iPadOS 18.2 and later, a person may select an app other than the Messages app to send instant messages.' The page covers only im: and sms: URL handling.

route: SMS/MMS message filter extension (IdentityLookup, ILMessageFilterExtension)
required_permission: The user enables the filter in Settings (flow not re-verified).
data_scope: Only SMS and MMS from unknown senders. It 'doesn't work with messages from senders in a user's Contacts list or with iMessage messages'.
restrictions: The extension 'can't access the network directly' and 'can't write data to containers shared with the containing app'.
next_experiment: None. It sees no messages from known contacts and cannot pass data to the app.
evidence_notes: The IdentityLookup docs limit filtering to unknown senders, exclude iMessage, and block both networking and writes to the shared container, by design for privacy.

route: Mac companion reading the Messages database (~/Library/Messages) with user-granted Full Disk Access
required_permission: Full Disk Access (a user-granted privacy setting) in an app that is not sandboxed, so it would ship with Developer ID outside the Mac App Store.
data_scope: Possibly the full Messages history synced to the Mac (iMessage plus relayed SMS). Not tested.
historical_coverage: Possibly the full history. Not tested.
refresh_cadence: Possibly near real time by watching the database. Not tested.
restrictions: DTS (March 2024): 'There's no API to do that. Moreover, the location and format of the message database is not considered API'. Mac App Store apps must be sandboxed (2.4.5(i)) and may not read outside their container (2.5.2). A search snippet says Full Disk Access does not lift sandbox restrictions.
next_experiment: Do not build. Treat it as a product and legal decision: it reads another app's undocumented private store and can't ship on the Mac App Store. If it is ever reconsidered, get legal review first.
evidence_notes: Full Disk Access is a real, user-granted permission, so this does not get around access control. But it depends on a private database format that Apple says is 'not considered API', and it can't pass App Store sandboxing. We class it as blocked: unsupported, not a sanctioned integration.

route: Mac companion scripting the Messages app with AppleScript (Apple Events)
required_permission: Automation (Apple Events) permission to control Messages. Sandbox and App Store implications not verified.
data_scope: Apple DTS says it is limited and probably does not expose individual messages.
restrictions: Not verified.
next_experiment: Optional one-hour check: open the Messages scripting dictionary on macOS 26 and confirm whether message content or timestamps are exposed.
evidence_notes: DTS: 'Messages has an AppleScript interface... I don't think it offers access to the individual messages', and in thread 804040 scripting Messages is 'quite limited'.

route: The user shares a screenshot or selected text of a conversation into LittleThings (share extension), with on-device Vision OCR
required_permission: None beyond the user choosing LittleThings in the share sheet.
data_scope: Only what the user chooses to share at that moment.
historical_coverage: Only what is visible or selected.
refresh_cadence: Manual and user-initiated every time. Never label it automatic monitoring.
restrictions: None found.
next_experiment: Build a share-extension spike that accepts images and text, run RecognizeTextRequest on a Messages screenshot in airplane mode, and measure how accurately sender and timestamp segments come out.
evidence_notes: A Share extension receives 'the user's initial text and any attachments'. RecognizeTextRequest recognizes text in an image (iOS 18+). The fetched page does not say it runs on-device.

route: WhatsApp per-chat 'Export chat' on iPhone, shared into LittleThings through the share sheet
required_permission: None from an API. The user exports each chat and picks LittleThings in the share sheet.
data_scope: One chat's text history, optionally with the most recent media as attachments. Search snippets describe a text file in one place and a ZIP in another.
historical_coverage: The chat history at export time. Message-count caps were not verified.
refresh_cadence: Manual, per chat. Must be labelled a manual import.
restrictions: Per chat and user-initiated. The export 'can't be re-imported because it's a text file and not a backup file'. Regional availability was not verified.
next_experiment: Export a one-to-one and a group chat, with and without media, from WhatsApp on iOS. Confirm a LittleThings share extension appears and what it receives (ZIP or .txt), document the line format and date-locale variants, and build the parser.
evidence_notes: Evidence comes only from search-result snippets of the WhatsApp FAQ (steps, the 'Without media' and 'Include media' options, 'the most recent media sent will be added as attachments'). The FAQ page itself returned only its title.

route: WhatsApp Business Platform (Cloud API)
required_permission: A Meta business portfolio and a business phone number registered on the platform.
data_scope: Messages that users send to the business's own number. It does not reach a person's personal WhatsApp chats.
restrictions: Business-only. 'the contents of any message sent from a WhatsApp user to your business phone number is communicated via webhook' and webhooks 'deliver JSON payloads to your server'.
next_experiment: None. It is the wrong product (business messaging) and needs a server.
evidence_notes: The Cloud API overview says 'You must have a business portfolio to use the platform' and that incoming messages arrive by webhook at your server.

route: Reading WhatsApp Mac or desktop app data from a Mac companion
required_permission: Not applicable.
data_scope: No public API found. Reading the desktop app's local store would put it in the same class as imessage-sms-mac-chatdb-fda (an undocumented private store).
historical_coverage: Per FAQ snippets, the desktop apps sync more history than WhatsApp Web, but the full history lives on the phone.
restrictions: An account-information report can't be requested from the Mac app (FAQ snippet).
next_experiment: None. For capture on the Mac, use user-initiated screen capture or the share/Services route instead.
evidence_notes: Only search-result snippets of WhatsApp FAQ pages were seen. No developer API for desktop chat data appeared in any source.

route: Mac companion: user-initiated capture through the system picker (SCContentSharingPicker, ScreenCaptureKit), then on-device Vision OCR
required_permission: Screen-recording permission with the NSScreenCaptureUsageDescription key. Whether capturing only through the picker avoids the Screen Recording permission prompt was not verified.
data_scope: Pixels of the window or display the user picks, at that moment.
historical_coverage: Only what is on screen at capture time.
restrictions: Must stay user-initiated for each capture to avoid hidden scraping. Whether provider terms allow capturing their web pages was not verified. Sandbox and App Store compatibility was not verified.
next_experiment: Spike on macOS 26: present SCContentSharingPicker, grab one frame of a Messages or WhatsApp window with SCScreenshotManager, and OCR it with RecognizeTextRequest offline. Record which permission prompts appear and whether a sandboxed build works.
evidence_notes: Apple says to 'Request screen recording permission from the person before capturing content' and recommends SCContentSharingPicker 'as the recommended approach for letting people select content sources'.

route: Mac companion reading other apps' on-screen text through the Accessibility (AX) API
required_permission: The Accessibility privilege (user-granted).
data_scope: The UI text of other apps.
refresh_cadence: Could run continuously, which is exactly the hidden-scraping pattern the product rules forbid.
restrictions: Search snippets attribute to Apple DTS: 'We do not support the Accessibility APIs in sandboxed apps' (not confirmed on an opened page). Developers report rejections under guideline 2.4.5 for non-accessibility uses. The Mac App Store requires sandboxing.
next_experiment: None. Use the picker-based capture or the share/Services route.
evidence_notes: DTS in thread 707680 points sandboxed apps to Input Monitoring for event taps (available 'even [to] apps published on the Mac App Store'). That does not help read UI text. The claim that Accessibility is unsupported in the sandbox comes from search snippets only.

route: Mac companion share extension or Services-menu item: the user selects text in any app and sends it to LittleThings
required_permission: None beyond the user invoking it.
data_scope: The text, links or images the user selects.
restrictions: None found. Services-menu behavior was not verified this session.
next_experiment: Build a macOS share extension plus an NSServices entry that accept text, and verify they appear for selections in Messages, WhatsApp and Safari on macOS 26.
evidence_notes: The extension context carries 'the user's initial text and any attachments for a post, such as links, images, or videos'.

route: User-initiated Safari Web Extension that captures the current page when the user clicks
required_permission: Not investigated.
data_scope: Not investigated.
restrictions: Provider terms on automated collection (LinkedIn, Meta) must be checked before any build. Not investigated.
next_experiment: Separate feasibility study: Safari Web Extension permission model (per-site grant on click), and LinkedIn's and Meta's terms on user-initiated page capture.
evidence_notes: Out of scope for this pass, per the brief: a separate feasibility path.

route: Apple Foundation Models on-device LLM (SystemLanguageModel)
required_permission: No user permission. Apple Intelligence must be enabled on an eligible device. iOS, iPadOS, macOS and visionOS 26+.
data_scope: On-device summarizing, entity extraction, classification and tagging (a contentTagging use case exists). Context of 4,096 tokens per session, counting instructions, prompts and outputs together.
refresh_cadence: Not applicable. One request at a time per session.
restrictions: 'Model availability depends on whether the device and region supports Apple Intelligence.' Unavailable reasons: deviceNotEligible, appleIntelligenceNotEnabled, modelNotReady. Check languages with supportedLanguages or supportsLocale(_:). The model changes with OS updates (versions 26.0-26.3, 26.4, 27.0). PrivateCloudComputeLanguageModel (iOS 27+) is an explicit opt-in server model; it breaks the no-cloud-AI rule and must not be used.
next_experiment: Run an availability and supportsLocale matrix on test devices (eligible, ineligible, Apple Intelligence off). Benchmark guided-generation 'life update' extraction on chunks of about 3.5k tokens, and design a rule-based fallback for ineligible devices.
evidence_notes: 'the system model supports up to 4,096 tokens'. The UnavailableReason enum has three cases. The PCC article says PCC is used only when a session is created with PrivateCloudComputeLanguageModel, and lists SystemLanguageModel as 'Works offline'.

route: On-device speech-to-text with SpeechAnalyzer and SpeechTranscriber (iOS 26+)
required_permission: Microphone permission for live capture (speech-permission requirements for this API not verified). Locale assets are installed through AssetInventory.
data_scope: Transcripts of live or file audio. Locales listed in the page metadata: de-DE, en-US, es-419, fr-FR, it-IT, ja-JP, ko-KR, pt-BR, zh-CN.
restrictions: SpeechTranscriber.isAvailable depends on 'the device's hardware and capabilities'. DictationTranscriber is the fallback for older devices. Too many concurrent analyses throw insufficientResources. The fetched pages do NOT say outright that processing stays on-device.
next_experiment: In airplane mode on iOS 26, install en-US assets through AssetInventory, transcribe a 2-minute voice note, and confirm it works without network. Repeat on an older device with DictationTranscriber.
evidence_notes: The API exists on iOS, iPadOS and macOS 26.0+, with installedLocales and supportedLocales checks and asset downloads. On-device-only processing is implied by the asset model but not stated on the pages fetched.

route: SFSpeechRecognizer with requiresOnDeviceRecognition = true, gated on supportsOnDeviceRecognition
required_permission: Speech-recognition and microphone permissions (keys not re-verified).
data_scope: Transcripts. 'on-device requests won't be as accurate.'
restrictions: The request honors requiresOnDeviceRecognition only if supportsOnDeviceRecognition is true. Otherwise 'the SFSpeechRecognizer requires a network', so the app must refuse to transcribe rather than fall back to the server.
next_experiment: Implement a hard gate: if supportsOnDeviceRecognition is false for the locale, disable voice capture. Test with en-US and one less common locale.
evidence_notes: requiresOnDeviceRecognition: 'Set this property to true to prevent an SFSpeechRecognitionRequest from sending audio over the network.'

route: Vision text recognition (RecognizeTextRequest; iOS 18+, macOS 15+)
required_permission: None.
data_scope: Text from images, with recognitionLanguages, automaticallyDetectsLanguage, usesLanguageCorrection and customWords settings.
restrictions: The fetched page does not state on-device processing, and it does not list language cases (see supportedRecognitionLanguages).
next_experiment: Run OCR on 20 chat screenshots in airplane mode, record accuracy and latency, and log supportedRecognitionLanguages on iOS 26.
evidence_notes: 'An image-analysis request that recognizes text in an image.' Available on iOS 18.0, macOS 15.0 and visionOS 2.0.

route: iOS and macOS Share extension receiving text, URLs, images and files from other apps
required_permission: None. The user picks the extension in the share sheet.
data_scope: 'the user's initial text and any attachments for a post, such as links, images, or videos'.
restrictions: The extension must 'Prepare to be terminated by the system'. The activation-rule docs could not be fetched (404), and memory limits were not verified.
next_experiment: Build a share extension that writes into an App Group container and test receiving WhatsApp export ZIPs, LinkedIn CSVs and screenshots.
evidence_notes: Apple's App Extension Programming Guide (archived) describes the Share extension context. Sending data to the containing app through App Groups is standard but was not re-verified this session.

route: MessageUI MFMessageComposeViewController (prefilled iMessage/SMS that the user sends)
required_permission: None. Check canSendText() first.
data_scope: Sends one prefilled message after the user approves it.
restrictions: It cannot send unattended: it 'only lets you construct the initial message and present it for a person's approval'. The delegate reports cancelled, sent or failed, and sent means 'The user successfully queued or sent the message' (not delivered). App Review 5.1.2(v) requires showing how the message will look to the recipient.
next_experiment: Use it for the 'reach out' action. Log only the sent, cancelled or failed result locally, and never treat sent as delivered.
evidence_notes: 'The composition interface doesn't guarantee the delivery of your message.' The MessageComposeResult.sent description says 'queued or sent'.

route: User-configured Shortcuts personal automation (for example Time of Day or Message trigger, then Send Message), with LittleThings supplying text through an App Intent
required_permission: The user builds the automation in the Shortcuts app and turns off 'Ask Before Running'. The app can't create it on the user's behalf (not verified, but no API for that was found).
data_scope: Whatever text the App Intent returns, sent by Shortcuts' Send Message action.
restrictions: The current Apple guide lists Time of Day, Message, Email and others among triggers that can run automatically, but warns 'You may also need to set individual actions to run automatically.' Whether Send Message runs without a prompt on iOS 26 is not verified; community reports conflict. App Review 5.1.2(v) still applies to app-initiated contact.
next_experiment: On an iOS 26 device, build a Time of Day automation (Ask Before Running off) that runs a test App Intent returning text into Send Message to a second test phone. Record any confirmation UI, the lock-screen behavior, and the result.
evidence_notes: Apple's guide: 'turn off Ask Before Running, then tap Don't Ask'. MacMost (2022, third party) shows a Time of Day plus Send Message automation sending without asking. This is the only possible unattended-send route that works outside the EU, and it is configured by the user, not the app.

route: Contacts limited access: ContactAccessButton and contactAccessPicker (iOS 18+)
required_permission: Works when authorization is .limited or none. The button doesn't appear when access is already full.
data_scope: Lets the person grant access to more individual contacts from inside the app's search UI.
restrictions: iOS, iPadOS and Mac Catalyst 18.0+.
next_experiment: Make limited access the default onboarding path, with ContactAccessButton bound to the 'add person' search field. Measure how many contacts users grant.
evidence_notes: 'If a single contact matches, the button shows that contact's name and image, and tapping the button grants your app access to that contact.' contactAccessPicker presents a picker of all contacts.

route: UNUserNotificationCenter local notifications: limit on pending requests
required_permission: Notification authorization.
data_scope: At most 64 pending or active notification requests per app.
refresh_cadence: The app must refill the queue opportunistically (on launch or in background tasks).
restrictions: The limit comes from an Apple engineer on the Developer Forums (January 2026), not from reference docs. Behavior when more than 64 are scheduled is unconfirmed.
next_experiment: Schedule only the nearest ~60 reminders and refill on launch and during BGAppRefresh. Add a test that schedules 70 and records which ones survive on iOS 26.
evidence_notes: An Apple engineer wrote: 'Yes, there is a limit of 64 for how many simultaneous notification requests can be active/pending at one time per app. This is a system limit and there is no way around it.'

route: BGTaskScheduler background refresh and processing
required_permission: Background-modes capability and registered task identifiers (not re-verified).
data_scope: Lets the app run code for sync, OCR or LLM batches while suspended.
refresh_cadence: Best effort: 'the system doesn't guarantee launching the task at the specified date, but only that it won't begin sooner.'
restrictions: Frequency, the effect of force-quit, and Low Power Mode behavior were not verified on the fetched pages. BGContinuedProcessingTaskRequest exists (referenced) but was not investigated.
next_experiment: Instrument BGAppRefreshTask and BGProcessingTask launch times on 3 test phones for 2 weeks, so the product never promises timely automatic capture.
evidence_notes: The earliestBeginDate docs state that execution time is not guaranteed.

route: Gift purchase by handing off to the merchant's own checkout (open the merchant URL in Safari or SFSafariViewController)
required_permission: None.
data_scope: Only the merchant URL leaves the app.
restrictions: Whether Apple Pay on the web works inside SFSafariViewController was not verified. The merchant is the payment party, so LittleThings needs no merchant ID or payment provider.
next_experiment: Open three common gift merchants' product pages in SFSafariViewController and confirm their Apple Pay web checkout is offered and completes.
evidence_notes: The planning page says the merchant or its payment provider decrypts and processes the payment token. With a handoff, that stays entirely with the merchant.

route: In-app Apple Pay, with LittleThings as the merchant
required_permission: A merchant ID, a payment processing certificate, and a payment service provider (PSP).
data_scope: Payment token plus shipping and contact details.
restrictions: 'Once decrypted, the token needs to be passed to the payment service provider for processing.' Decryption is done 'by the merchant with the certificate private key or by the Payment Service Provider'. Goods rules are in App Review 3.1, which was not checked on the fetched page.
next_experiment: None unless LittleThings becomes a merchant. Record the PSP and merchant processing as a backend dependency.
evidence_notes: The planning page describes the encrypted payment token going to the merchant or PSP for decryption and processing, so it needs either the merchant's own server or a third-party PSP backend.
